description: Our team is focused on building solutions that has meaning and creates an impact on our beautiful world
summary:
For over two decades, NASA satellites have tracked Earth's fire activity. But the record is changing hands. Older MODIS sensors and newer VIIRS sensors don't see fires the same way. VIIRS detects smaller hotspots, often reporting several times more detections in the same place and month. Without accounting for this difference, switching satellites can make burning appear to surge even when the underlying activity hasn't.

Fire Record Atlas bridges these two records. Explore an interactive globe of seasonal fire activity, discover regional burning patterns, and see how individual years compare with history. Atlas converts VIIRS detections to Aqua MODIS's scale using region and season specific calibration, with uncertainty ranges that show how much confidence to place in each estimate.

But can we trust the conversion? Our Satellite Time Machine lets visitors test it: predict a real observation withheld from the method, then reveal what Aqua actually recorded. 

Atlas explores how we can preserve a comparable historical fire record as satellites change, while making the limits of that comparison visible.

The real danger isn't losing the numbers. It's losing what they mean. As satellites change, we risk mistaking changes in what we can observe for changes in what's actually happening on Earth. Atlas helps us tell the difference, and makes clear when we can't.
details:
Fire Record Atlas is an interactive website for exploring 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections, and for seeing how far that record can be trusted when the satellites watching it change.

You start with a globe. Pick a month and the planet's fire belt lights up, shifting north and south with the seasons. Choose one of nine study regions and you get its burning calendar: which months are usually busiest, the normal range for each month, and whether a particular year ran above, within or below that range. This turns a large archive into a question anyone can ask: was this season unusual?

The difficulty is that the record is changing hands. The older MODIS sensors are near retirement, and the newer VIIRS sensors see in finer detail, so they catch smaller, cooler fires. In the same place and month, VIIRS often reports several times more hotspots. Without accounting for that difference, a change in satellite can look like a change in burning.

So we studied years when both satellites watched the same regions and learned how their counts relate. That relationship differs by region and season, because a savanna fire and a crop-burning fire look different from space, so we calibrated it separately for each. Atlas then converts a VIIRS count onto Aqua MODIS's scale and always shows a likely range, because a converted number is an estimate, not a measurement.

We tested the method against observations it had not seen. We hid real MODIS months from the method, converted the VIIRS counts, and only then compared. In our main test, covering five regions from 2018 to 2021, 200 of 215 hidden months landed inside the predicted 90% range. An earlier test with an older VIIRS satellite left two regions, Punjab–Haryana and the Central African Republic, marked provisional.

Our favourite part is the Satellite Time Machine. Instead of reading an accuracy figure, you run the test yourself: see the raw VIIRS count, convert it, then reveal what MODIS actually recorded. You can also step through other hidden months, including the misses.

We built Atlas as a static website in JavaScript, HTML and CSS, using D3 for the maps and charts. Python, DuckDB and Parquet files process the NASA FIRMS archives for MODIS and VIIRS. Automated tests and browser checks verify the published numbers.

Throughout, we kept measured values visibly separate from estimates, and we mark missing observations separately from months with zero detections. A hotspot detection is not a single fire or a measure of burned area. Aqua's orbit has drifted, so comparisons from 2022 onwards stay marked untested. Atlas cannot promise the record continues perfectly after MODIS, but it shows clearly where a comparison holds and where it still needs work.
